Concept

Overview

Vigil is a safety command platform concept for emergency control rooms. It links alerts from wearables and apps to the nearest verified responders, and escalates automatically when nobody answers. I designed the web dashboard and the mobile companion on my own over three months.

MY ROLE

Sole product designer, from research to developer-ready handoff

Mapped the operator workflow and the escalation logic

48 hi-fi frames in light and dark mode, built on design tokens

Every state and spec documented, so it can be built as drawn

The problem

One emergency, five tools — and nobody sure who’s on it.

Control-room operators handled a single SOS across five separate systems. Every switch cost seconds — and no screen showed which alert had nobody on it.

Persona

PERSONA

Martin

Control-room operator

Needs three answers in seconds: what’s happening, who’s on it, what do I do next?

01

Ownership is invisible

No tool showed who was handling an alert, so two people could take the same SOS — or nobody would.

02

Switching costs the most time

Most seconds were lost moving between tools, not making decisions.

03

Escalation depends on memory

If nobody answered, escalating relied on someone noticing and remembering.

Key decisions

01

One view, three zones

Why: Live feed → Situation → Action reads like a sentence, so operators stop rebuilding the picture from five tools.

02

Actions on every alert card

Why: Call, assign and escalate sit right on the card — no context switch under stress.

03

Nobody waits

Why: A 5-step timer escalates an unanswered SOS automatically, from 0 seconds to 5 minutes.

Accessibility & privacy

Accessible by default

✓ WCAG 2.1 AA colour contrast

✓ Light and dark mode for 24/7 shifts

✓ Status never shown by colour alone

Privacy by design (GDPR)

✓ Live location shown only during an active SOS

✓ Only the data an operator needs to act

✓ Clear audit trail of who did what

Outcome

Self-initiated concept

It isn’t live, so there are no real numbers to share. Based on the workflow, I expect time-to-act to drop from about 12 minutes to 3.

After launch, I’d track

01

02

03

Steps it takes to escalate

What I learned

01

Test the alert card earlier

It changed the most between rounds. A quick test with operators at the wireframe stage would have saved time.

02

Design the empty and failure states first

The hardest moments — no responder, no signal — shaped the whole layout more than the happy path.

03

Concepts need a plan to prove them

That’s why the test plan is part of this case study: 5 operators, timed against the old workflow.
